name: Abelard's 'Sic et Non' and the value of dialectic
plain_explanation: In 'Sic et Non' ('Yes and No'), Abelard laid out dialectical arguments on both sides of many theological questions, often without resolving them, apparently valuing the exercise of disputation itself as sharpening the intellect. He held that, apart from Scripture, dialectic is the sole road to truth, and that nothing outside Scripture -- not even Apostles or Church Fathers -- is infallible.
precise_definition: Abelard's 1121-22 work presenting opposed authoritative quotations and arguments on a wide range of theological questions, used pedagogically to train critical, disputatious reasoning rather than to hand down settled doctrine.
why_it_mattered: It had, in Russell's words, 'a valuable effect as a solvent of prejudices and an encouragement to the fearless use of the intellect,' helping to wake people from 'dogmatic slumbers,' even though Russell notes 'no empiricist' could accept Abelard's claim that dialectic alone (barring Scripture) is the sole road to truth.
examples: Abelard's derivation of Logic's dignity from the opening of Saint John's Gospel ('In the beginning was the Logos')
objections: Russell's judgment that valuing logic as 'pre-eminently the Christian science' is, from a modern standpoint, excessive
competing_positions: Saint Bernard's mysticism, which sought truth in contemplation rather than disputation
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Contributed to Abelard's repeated condemnations for unorthodoxy (Soissons 1121, Sens 1141), driven, Russell suggests, more by his personal combativeness than by genuine heresy.
